blurb: Learning by trial and error: rewards, Atari, AlphaGo's famous moves, and taking it out of games into the real world.

cards.title: Trial and error, done by a computer

steps.p: Reinforcement learning has an agent (the learner) in an environment (a game, a robot's room). It acts, the world changes, and it sometimes gets a reward.

items: Agent adjusts what it does next time

steps.p: Unlike learning from examples, nobody says what the right move was. The agent only learns from how much reward it eventually gets.
steps.analogy: Training a dog with treats: you can't explain "sit", you just reward it when it happens.

steps.p: Agents aim for the most total reward, with future rewards counted slightly less — a "discount". At 0.99 per step, a reward 100 steps away is worth about 37% of one now.
Should it use the best move it knows, or try something new that might be better? Too little exploring and it never finds better options.
steps.analogy: Your favourite restaurant vs trying the new place that might be even better.

steps.p: When a reward comes after many moves, which ones earned it? That's the credit assignment problem — the heart of RL's difficulty.

cards.q: The explore–exploit trade-off is about choosing between…
options: Trying new actions to learn more vs using the best action known so far
cards.hint: The favourite restaurant vs the new one.
cards.why: Learn more vs cash in. Explore too little and you miss better options; too much and you waste time on bad ones.

cards.statement: In reinforcement learning, the agent is told the correct action at each step.
cards.why: False. It only gets rewards, often long after the action. Working out which actions were good is its job.

cards.q: With a discount of 0.99 per step, a reward 100 steps away is worth about what fraction of an immediate one?
cards.why: About 37%. 0.99 multiplied by itself 100 times ≈ 0.37. Distant rewards still count, just less.

cards.title: In 1992, TD-Gammon taught itself backgammon to near world-champion level by playing against itself.
cards.detail: Gerald Tesauro's network learned from self-play alone, and even changed how human experts played some opening moves.

options: Which of many earlier actions deserve credit for a later reward
Which researcher gets credit for a paper
cards.why: Which moves mattered? A chess win comes at the end; the brilliant move might have been 30 turns earlier.

cards.title: DQN: learning games from the screen

steps.p: In 2013–15 DeepMind's DQN learned dozens of Atari games from just the screen pixels and the score — no game rules given.
The network estimates a Q-value for each possible move: how much total future reward it expects from making that move now.
steps.analogy: Like a sat-nav estimating the remaining journey time for each possible turn.

steps.p: Learning from consecutive frames is unstable because they're so similar. DQN stores past experiences and learns from a random mix of them.
It also learns against a slowly updated copy of itself, so it isn't chasing a target that moves with every step.
Games with rare rewards stumped it. In Montezuma's Revenge, random button-pressing almost never finds any points to learn from.

cards.statement: DQN used the same design and settings across all 49 Atari games it was tested on.
cards.why: True. That was the breakthrough: one general learner, not 49 hand-built programs. It beat human testers on many games.

cards.q: Why does replaying old experiences help training?
options: Learning from a random mix breaks up the strong similarity between consecutive frames
It makes the game run faster
cards.why: Less lopsided learning. Thirty nearly identical frames in a row would push the network too hard one way. A random mix gives balanced lessons.

options: The total future reward expected from taking an action in a situation
cards.hint: Like a sat-nav's time estimate for each turn.
cards.why: Expected future reward. Pick the action with the highest Q-value and you're picking what it thinks will pay off most.

cards.title: The original DQN scored zero on Montezuma's Revenge.
cards.detail: The game needs long sequences of precise moves before any reward appears. Random exploration almost never found points, making it a famous benchmark for exploration.

cards.statement: Rare rewards make reinforcement learning easier.
cards.why: False. With rare rewards the agent gets almost no signal about what's working. Frequent feedback makes learning much easier.

steps.p: Go has more possible board positions than atoms in the observable universe. Checking every move, as chess programs partly did, is hopeless.
AlphaGo combined two networks — one suggesting promising moves, one judging who's winning — with a search that plays out likely futures.
steps.analogy: A strong player's gut instinct narrowing the options, then careful reading of a few lines.

steps.p: Monte Carlo tree search explores promising move sequences many times, guided by the networks, to pick the best move.
AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1. Its Move 37 in game two was so unusual experts first thought it was a mistake.
AlphaGo Zero learned purely by playing itself, from scratch, and beat the original. MuZero then learned even without being told the rules.

cards.q: AlphaGo's Move 37 in game two was striking because…
options: Its own estimate said a human would play it only about 1 in 10,000 times — yet it was strong
cards.why: Unhuman but brilliant. It showed the system had found ideas beyond human tradition, not just copied them.

cards.statement: AlphaGo Zero learned from databases of human games.
cards.why: False. It started from random play and learned only by playing itself — and became stronger than the version trained on human games.

cards.title: Lee Sedol won one game against AlphaGo, with a brilliant move later called "the divine move".
cards.detail: His Move 78 in game four confused AlphaGo. He retired in 2019, saying AI was "an entity that cannot be defeated".

options: Learning to plan without being told the game's rules
cards.why: No rulebook. It learned its own internal model of how the game works, then planned with it — mastering Go, chess and Atari.

cards.q: What role did tree search play in AlphaGo?
options: Looking ahead by simulating promising move sequences, guided by the networks
cards.hint: Look at the flow in step 3.
cards.why: Looking ahead. The networks gave instinct; the search checked those instincts by playing out futures.

steps.p: Real robots break and real time is slow, so agents practise millions of times in a simulated world first.
Simulations are never perfect — friction, lighting, motors differ. A policy that works in simulation can fail in reality.
steps.analogy: Learning to drive in a video game, then getting into a real car.

steps.p: Domain randomisation varies the simulation wildly — weights, colours, friction — so the real world looks like just another variation.
RL has cut data-center cooling energy, beaten world champions at the video game Dota 2, and controlled robot hands.
RL is also how chatbots learn from feedback (RLHF) and how reasoning models learn to think — see Days 7 and 12.

cards.q: DeepMind's RL system cut energy used for cooling Google's data centers by up to…
cards.why: Up to 40%. It learned better settings for fans, pumps and chillers than human operators' rules.

cards.statement: OpenAI Five beat the reigning world-champion team at the video game Dota 2.
cards.why: True. In April 2019 it beat OG, then world champions, after training on the equivalent of thousands of years of games against itself.

options: Varying the simulation widely so the policy copes with real-world differences
Making the robot move randomly forever
cards.hint: Look at the cells in step 3.
cards.why: Prepared for anything. If it has handled a thousand slightly different worlds, the real one is just one more.

cards.title: OpenAI trained a robot hand to solve a Rubik's Cube using only simulated practice.
cards.detail: The 2019 project relied on heavy domain randomisation. The hand still succeeded only part of the time on the hardest scrambles — showing how hard the real world is.

cards.title: Spot reward hacking at work
cards.body: People game metrics too: call centres rushing calls to hit a time target, or schools teaching to the test.
cards.challenge: Think of one target at your work or school. How could someone hit the number without achieving the real goal?
